Estimation of Partial Pressure of CO2 in the Coastal Waterbody using Satellite Data and Machine Learning Techniques

Abstract:

Estimating carbon dioxide (CO2) and associated CO2 fluxes in coastal water bodies is an important part of the global carbon cycle. Emissions of CO2 to the atmosphere depend largely on the partial pressure of CO2 (pCO2) in the surface water however, measured pCO2 data are scarce, and calculated pCO2 can show large uncertainty. The pCO2 is highly variable as it is controlled by several physical, chemical, and biological processes. Further, the coastal waterbodies are dynamic due to the interaction of fresh river water and saline ocean water. Thus, continuous and long-term monitoring of pCO2 is highly challenging. It has been found that recent advancements in machine learning techniques, in combination with in-situ observations and remote sensing techniques, have enabled accurate estimation of surface water pCO2. Thus, this study aims a comprehensive analysis of various physicochemical and biological parameters along with pCO2 in the Chilika lagoon. The in-situ pCO2, salinity, pH, and other water quality concentrations were measured during the summer, monsoon, and winter seasons of 2024-25 in order to understand their spatio-temporal variability in the lagoon. The surface water salinity and pH varied in the range of 0.10-31.05 ppt and 4.05-10.07, respectively. The concentration of pCO2 in the lagoon ranged from 5 to 8864 &microatm, with the highest pCO2 levels associated with the monsoon period, whereas the summer period showed low pCO2 concentration. The findings of this study will provide valuable insights for long-term monitoring of surface water pCO2 in the complex coastal waterbodies, and assessing their contribution to the global carbon budget.
